plan.title: perf(release): step 3 makes one sequential gh call per anchored issue (1,156 today) and grows with project history

narratives.Description: perf(release): step 3 makes one sequential gh call per anchored issue (1,156 today) and grows with project history
narratives.Overview:
## Summary

Release step 3 (`Pre-flight vBRIEF lifecycle sync`) issues **one `gh api` subprocess per anchored issue, strictly sequentially, with no batching and no concurrency**. On this repository that is **1,156 calls**, and it ran 38+ minutes on a single release attempt while still in step 3 of 13.

The cost scales linearly with the number of briefs ever created, and the brief corpus only grows.

Recut after a design critique (successor lean 5420863915). The mechanism and the growth property stand. **The remedy changed**: an open-only paginated fetch removes the need to narrow the check at all, so the terminal-prefiltering direction originally preferred here is no longer the plan.

## The mechanism

`packages/core/src/intake/reconcile-issues.ts:340-350`

```ts
for (const n of sortedNumbers) {
  const fetched = fetchOneIssueStateRest(owner, name, n, scmCall, options.cwd ?? undefined);
  if (fetched === "CLI_MISSING") { ... }
  if (fetched === null) { return null; }
  states.set(n, fetched);
}
```

Called from `checkVbriefLifecycleSyncNative` (`packages/core/src/release/native-steps.ts`), which builds the anchor set by scanning every brief in the lifecycle root. Step 3 deduplicates scanner output before fetching (`native-steps.ts:55-65`). No pagination, no list call, no batch, no parallelism — one process spawn, one HTTP round-trip, one issue.

## Measured, this repository, at `c784755f`

Derived by calling `scanLifecycleAnchors("./xbrief")` directly rather than reimplementing its rule:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Anchor rows | 1,387 |
| Rows carrying an issue | 1,354 |
| **Unique issue numbers → one `gh` call each** | **1,156** |
| Rows with no issue anchor (cause no fetch) | 33 |
| Bare `gh api .../issues/N` on this machine | ~0.615 s |
| Actual elapsed in step 3 | 38 min, still running |

**Correction:** an earlier revision of this issue said 1,252. That was wrong. The production resolver returns 1,156 unique anchors, and every duration or ratio derived from 1,252 was off by 96 calls.

**Rate limiting is not the cause** — `gh api rate_limit` reports `core: 5000/5000`, and no `[release Step 3] GitHub REST rate limit hit` line appears in the log. The loop is simply doing 1,156 sequential round-trips, each paying process spawn plus network.

## Why it gets worse forever

The anchor set derives from the brief corpus, and briefs are never removed — completed and cancelled ones stay tracked by design, since #3476 requires the completed artifact to land. Each shipped story permanently adds one more sequential call to every future release. A check whose cost grows with project history, on the critical path of shipping, eventually makes releasing impractical rather than merely slow.

## What the check is for

It finds briefs still in a non-terminal folder whose issue is closed — lifecycle drift. `buildLifecycleReport` partitions each anchored row solely on `state === "OPEN"` (`reconcile-issues.ts:619-668`), and step 3 reports only non-terminal paths from `no_open_issue` (`native-steps.ts:70-87`). Its mismatch set is exactly:

> anchor has a non-open issue **AND** anchor path is non-terminal

The objection is entirely to how it gathers state.

## The remedy: one open-only paginated fetch

Measured against the live repository:

| Approach | Pages | Rows | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `state=all&per_page=100` | 38 | 3,744 | 29.8 s |
| **`state=open&per_page=100`** | **6** | **558** | **4.2 s**, one subprocess |

Feeding the open-number set to the production scanner's 32 non-terminal anchor rows reproduced the same verdict: 29 unique candidate issues, zero mismatches.

So: fetch the complete open-issue inventory in one paginated REST subprocess, retain the **full** anchor set, and treat any anchored issue absent from that inventory as non-open. This keeps every anchor the check has today, avoids any coverage-narrowing argument, and is measured at a 7x margin over the all-state alternative — which still scales with total history and would miss this issue's own acceptance criterion.

`packages/core/src/cache/fetch.ts:320-365` already contains a bounded pull-filtering REST issue-list implementation defaulting to open, though it currently spawns once per page rather than once for the whole pagination.

**The load-bearing safety property moves.** Treating absence-from-inventory as non-open means a truncated or malformed inventory silently marks open issues as closed and inverts the gate. The replacement must fail closed on command failure, malformed or non-array pages, pagination exhaustion, and output-buffer exhaustion, and must ignore pull-request rows.

## Why terminal prefiltering is no longer the plan

It would have worked, and it was measured as a large win: 1,322 of 1,354 anchored rows are terminal, and **1,127 of 1,156 unique issue numbers are reachable only from terminal rows (97.491%)**. But it is not needed, and it carries two costs the open-list approach avoids:

1. It leaves 29 sequential subprocesses.
2. It narrows what a fail-closed check inspects, which under #3156 requires proving coverage is preserved.

And that proof is narrower than it first appears. Filtering terminal rows preserves *step 3's current* mismatch set, but the general claim "terminal briefs cannot be lifecycle-drifted" is **false** — a completed brief whose issue is still open is reverse drift; this gate simply does not test for it. The equivalence would break the moment step 3 covered reverse drift, consulted terminal issue state, exposed report totals, or filtered issue numbers instead of rows.

There is also a trap for anyone who revisits it: exactly **one issue number is shared between a terminal and a non-terminal row**, so an implementation that subtracts every issue seen in a terminal row would wrongly drop it. Rows must be filtered before issue numbers are deduplicated.

Keep prefiltering in reserve only if the open-list baseline is measured inadequate.

## Escape hatch, currently undiscoverable

`--allow-vbrief-drift` skips step 3 entirely (`packages/core/src/release/pipeline.ts:161-162`). It is **not listed** in the task usage line, which advertises only:

```
task release -- <version> [--dry-run] [--skip-tag] [--skip-release] [--no-draft]
```

An operator watching a release stall has no way to learn the flag exists without reading the source.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Step 3 gathers issue state via a single open-only paginated REST subprocess, not one call per anchor
- [ ] The full anchor set is retained; no anchor is dropped before evaluation
- [ ] The inventory read fails closed on command failure, malformed or non-array pages, pagination exhaustion, and buffer exhaustion; pull-request rows are ignored
- [ ] Step 3 still detects a non-terminal brief whose issue is closed — no coverage lost (#3156)
- [ ] Step 3 completes in time proportional to open-issue count rather than total project history
- [ ] The step reports progress, or at minimum an up-front count of what it intends to check
- [ ] `--allow-vbrief-drift` appears in the task usage line
- [ ] CHANGELOG `[Unreleased]` line

## Out of scope

- A parallel worker pool. Dropped: it adds ordering and partial-failure complexity with no evidence it is needed after a 4.2 second measurement.
- Terminal prefiltering, unless the open-list baseline proves inadequate.
- Whether step 3 should also detect reverse drift (a terminal brief with an open issue). Genuinely uncovered today, but a scope increase rather than a speedup.

## Environment

Windows 11; process spawn here is roughly 5-10x normal (bare `node -e "0"` at 340 ms), so absolute timings are inflated. The 1,156 sequential round-trips and the linear-growth property are machine-independent.

Related: #3673 (same defect class, already fixed for `verify:completed-tracked` via a single `git cat-file --batch`), #3476 (why the corpus grows monotonically), #3156 (gate integrity).

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-26T03:50:52Z)

## Amendment: 97.2% of the calls cannot possibly find a mismatch

Measured the anchor set against the folder each brief lives in. The check filters terminal paths out of its **results** (`isTerminalLifecyclePath`), but fetches their GitHub state first.

| Folder | Briefs |
|---|---|
| `completed/` | 1330 |
| `cancelled/` | 25 |
| `proposed/` | 32 |
| other | 3 |

| Anchor class | Count |
|---|---|
| Reachable **only** from terminal briefs (`completed/`, `cancelled/`) | **1217** |
| Reachable from a non-terminal brief -- the only ones that can drift | **35** |
| Share of calls that cannot possibly produce a finding | **97.2%** |

A brief in `completed/` or `cancelled/` is terminal by definition and is discarded from the report regardless of what GitHub says about its issue. Its state is fetched anyway.

**So the step spends ~38 minutes making 1252 round-trips in order to evaluate 35 candidates.** At the measured ~1.82s per call, the necessary work is about **64 seconds**.

This makes Direction 2 the obvious first move and reframes it: it is not an optimisation, it is removing calls whose results are thrown away. Filter the anchor set by `isTerminalLifecyclePath` **before** `fetchIssueStatesForRelease` rather than after, and the same check produces the same verdict from 35 calls instead of 1252 -- roughly a 35x reduction with no coverage change, no batching, and no concurrency needed.

Batching (Direction 1) would still help the residual and is worth doing, but it is no longer the load-bearing fix.

Also note the growth property gets sharper: the 1217 wasted calls are exactly the ones that accumulate forever, because #3476 requires completed artifacts to stay tracked. The *useful* 35 stays roughly constant with WIP. So today's ratio is not a plateau -- the waste fraction climbs toward 100% as the project ages.

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-26T03:55:18Z)

## Correction to the amendment above -- numbers restated from the real code path

I derived the previous amendment's figures with my own script that collected **every** `plan.references` entry. That is not what the code does. `resolveLifecycleAnchor` (`reconcile-issues.ts:503-527`) resolves **one** anchor per brief, in priority order: `planRef`, then `parent_issue`, then the first GitHub-issue reference excluding the decomposition origin.

Re-derived by calling `scanLifecycleAnchors` directly:

| Quantity | My estimate | **Actual** |
|---|---|---|
| Unique issue numbers fetched | 1252 | **1156** |
| Anchors only from terminal briefs | 1217 | **1127** |
| Anchors from non-terminal briefs | 35 | **29** |
| Share that cannot produce a finding | 97.2% | **97.5%** |

Anchor axis breakdown: `references` 1219, `parent_issue` 95, `planRef` 40.

**The conclusion is unchanged and slightly stronger** -- 1156 sequential calls to evaluate 29 candidates, 97.5% of them structurally incapable of producing a finding.

## Retracting a false drift claim

I also reported finding 5 lifecycle mismatches. **That was wrong** and is withdrawn. It was an artifact of the same error: a brief for #3598 that *mentions* closed #1502 in its body looked drifted, when its actual anchor is #3598, which is open.

Running the real check over the 29 genuine anchors: **zero drift**. Every non-terminal brief's anchor issue is open. Step 3 would have passed -- it simply needed ~1 hour of sequential round-trips to report a clean result.

That sharpens the acceptance case rather than weakening it. The step spent an hour to answer a question that takes **20 seconds** when scoped to the anchors that can actually drift, and the answer was "nothing wrong".

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-26T03:58:12Z)

## The decisive number: the rest of the release takes 60 seconds

I killed the stalled run at 50 minutes (still in step 3, nothing mutating had happened) and re-ran with `--allow-vbrief-drift`, having performed step 3's actual check by hand first.

**The remaining twelve steps completed in 60 seconds.** That includes a full local `task check`, the CHANGELOG and ROADMAP promotion, a dist build, the tag, an atomic push, and GitHub release creation.

```
[3/13] Pre-flight vBRIEF lifecycle sync... SKIP (--allow-vbrief-drift)
[5/13] Pre-flight CI (task ci:local | fallback task check)... OK
...
Release v0.107.0 pipeline complete   <- 60s wall, total
```

So the shape of a release today is roughly **one minute of work wrapped around an hour of step 3**, and step 3's verdict was "nothing wrong".

The manual equivalent of the check -- resolve anchors via `scanLifecycleAnchors`, keep the 29 from non-terminal briefs, query those -- took **20 seconds** and returned the same answer.

| | Time | Calls |
|---|---|---|
| Step 3 as implemented | >50 min, did not finish | 1156 |
| Same question, anchors scoped to non-terminal briefs | **20s** | **29** |
| Entire rest of the release pipeline | **60s** | -- |

v0.107.0 shipped this way: tag `c784755f`, npm `0.107.0` live, GitHub release public.

### Comment by @MScottAdams (2026-08-26T04:50:02Z)

## Triage

mechanism-shaped: true

design-critique: warranted, because the leading direction narrows what a fail-closed check inspects in order to make it fast, which is precisely the shape #3156 treats as suspect unless the narrowing is proved coverage-preserving. The performance claim is measured; the safety claim behind the preferred remedy is asserted.

refutation-target: terminal briefs in `completed/` and `cancelled/` cannot be lifecycle-drifted, so filtering them before the state fetch loses no coverage.

## Non-self-arbitration disclosure

I filed this issue and I am running its triage. Under Decorrelation and Non-self-arbitration I may not clear my own claims. The refutation target above is my own asserted premise, chosen deliberately as the thing most likely to be wrong and most expensive if it is.

## Audit markers

- `audit:call-count` — the body states **1252** unique anchors. My own working note from the same night records **1156**. At least one is wrong; both were produced by me. Do not adopt either figure without re-deriving it from `scanLifecycleAnchors`. I previously produced a false finding on this issue by reimplementing that function's rule instead of calling it, and retracted it in-thread.
- `audit:terminal-share` — the claim that "most of the corpus is terminal," which is what makes direction 2 a large win, is unmeasured in the body.
- `audit:drift-definition` — whether `isTerminalLifecyclePath` filtering *results* is semantically equivalent to filtering *inputs* depends on what the check considers drift. A brief sitting in `completed/` whose issue is still open is not obviously outside the check's remit.

## What is solid

The mechanism is directly cited and simple: `reconcile-issues.ts:340-350` is a bare sequential loop with one subprocess per anchor, no batching, no pool. Rate limiting is ruled out by a `core: 5000/5000` reading and the absence of the rate-limit log line. The monotonic-growth property follows from #3476 requiring completed artifacts to stay tracked, and is machine-independent even where the absolute timings are inflated by Windows process spawn.

The undiscoverable `--allow-vbrief-drift` escape hatch is a separate, small, and independently shippable defect.

## What the critique should press on

Beyond the refutation target: whether direction 1 (one paginated list call) makes direction 2 unnecessary, which would let the check keep its full anchor set and moot the coverage question entirely. The body prefers the narrowing remedy without establishing that the non-narrowing one is inadequate.

## Thread repair — my comments posted as literal file paths

Every parent comment I posted to this arc before this one landed as the single literal string `@C:\Users\msada\AppData\Local\Temp\...`, not as its content. Cause: I used `gh api ... -f body=@<file>`. The `-f` / `--raw-field` flag posts a string literal and performs no `@` file expansion; that is `-F` / `--field`, or the form this repository's own guidance specifies, `gh issue comment <N> --body-file <path>`. I verified the correct form against a scratch comment before repairing.

All affected comments have been reposted with their real content and the stubs deleted. Thirteen stubs in total across this cluster.

## Consequence for the critics already dispatched

The critics on this arc were dispatched with an id ceiling pointing at one of those stubs, so **the thread carried them nothing** — the Stop 1 write-back, the charter and spend record, and the reopening corrections were all unreadable at the ceiling.

Their critiques are still valid, because the dispatch envelope carried that content directly: the refutation target where the charter was refutation, the withdrawn claims where there were withdrawals, the SHA, the round, and the audit targets. What they lost was the ability to read it a second time in the thread. One critic noticed and reported it as a finding, which is the correct behaviour and is now on the record twice over.

I am not re-running any critic that already posted. Re-dispatching for a defect in the parent's plumbing would spend a retry slot on nothing, and the contract reserves reiteration for residual disagreement.

## My own dispatch instruction was the propagation vector

The envelope I sent each critic told it to post using `gh api ... -f body=@<path>`. That instruction was wrong, and one critic followed it faithfully — its comment posted as a path stub. Its findings were recovered verbatim from its output file and posted unmodified, with provenance disclosed on that comment. Later dispatches in this cluster use `--body-file`.

Recording this as a parent process defect rather than quietly fixing it: a parent that hands workers a broken command turns one mistake into N.

class: `sharpens-framing`

audit:terminal-share: resolved

Concrete failure mode: saying only that "most of the corpus is terminal" conflates artifact rows with unique network calls and hides the shared-anchor case. An implementation that subtracts every issue number seen in a terminal row would incorrectly remove the one shared issue.

Disposition consequence: the large-win premise survives, but state it using the call denominator and require row filtering first, then issue-number deduplication. The supported claim is 1,127 avoidable calls and 29 retained unique issue numbers, not 1,217/35 or 1,252 total.

## The refutation target survives only for Step 3's current invariant

class: `sharpens-framing`

audit:drift-definition: resolved

Evidence: `buildLifecycleReport` partitions each anchored row solely on `state === "OPEN"` (`packages/core/src/intake/reconcile-issues.ts:619-668`). Step 3 then reports only non-terminal paths from `no_open_issue` and defines its failure as a closed/nonexistent issue brief outside `completed/` or `cancelled/` (`packages/core/src/release/native-steps.ts:70-87`). Therefore its mismatch set is exactly:

`anchor has a non-open issue AND anchor path is non-terminal`.

Filtering terminal anchor rows before state lookup preserves that set. It also preserves the shared-anchor case if rows are filtered before deduplication.

Concrete failure mode: the broader sentence "terminal briefs cannot be lifecycle-drifted" is false as a general lifecycle definition. A completed brief whose issue remains open can be reverse drift, but this gate does not test that invariant: it classifies the row as linked and returns no mismatch. The equivalence would break if Step 3 later covered reverse drift, used terminal issue state/reason, exposed report totals, or filtered issue numbers rather than anchor rows.

Disposition consequence: the refutation target survives for the current gate, but narrow the claim to: "terminal anchor rows cannot contribute to Step 3's closed-issue/non-terminal mismatch set." What would have broken it is any terminal-state invariant in Step 3's acceptance or any consumer of terminal rows beyond the discarded report entries.

class: `blocks-the-design`

Evidence: I measured the REST list alternatives against the live repository. `state=all&per_page=100` required 38 pages / 3,744 rows and 29.8 seconds, so the body's literal all-state direction still scales with project history. `state=open&per_page=100` required **6 pages / 558 rows and 4.2 seconds** in one `gh api --paginate --slurp` subprocess. Concrete failure mode: binding the preferred remedy as terminal prefiltering leaves 29 sequential subprocesses and accepts a coverage-narrowing proof burden that is unnecessary. Binding the body’s all-state list literally keeps total-history scaling and misses its own acceptance criterion.

Disposition consequence: the preferred remedy cannot bind as written. Baseline the non-narrowing design as one fail-closed, open-only paginated REST subprocess; treat every anchored issue absent from the complete open inventory as non-open, while retaining the full anchor set for report evaluation. Use terminal prefiltering only if that baseline is shown inadequate.

Road not taken: an all-state list is semantically direct but measured worse and history-scaled. The strongest case for terminal prefiltering is its small patch and 97.49% reduction; it would regain preference if the open-list endpoint could not provide a bounded, parse-complete, fail-closed inventory or measured materially slower in the release seam.

class: `footnote`

The list payload is external JSON, so the replacement must fail closed on command failure, malformed/non-array pages, pagination exhaustion, and output-buffer exhaustion; it must also ignore pull-request rows. A worker pool would add ordering and partial-failure complexity without evidence it is needed after the 4.2-second open-list measurement.

Critic: `gpt-5.6-sol-medium` (5420818794). One of one posted. Stop 2 record 5420776642.

> Terminal briefs in `completed/` and `cancelled/` cannot be lifecycle-drifted, so filtering them before the state fetch loses no coverage.

The critic resolved all three audit markers by measurement and then made the target moot by finding a better design. That is the best possible outcome for an arc and the worst possible outcome for my preferred remedy.

## Audit markers — all three resolved

**`audit:call-count` — resolved. The body is wrong; the count is 1,156.**

The critic called `scanLifecycleAnchors("./xbrief")` directly rather than reimplementing its rule: 1,387 anchor rows, 1,354 with an issue, **1,156 unique issue numbers**. The body's 1,252 overstates the fetch count by 96 and makes every derived duration and reduction ratio computed from it wrong.

This is the marker I flagged because my own working note said 1,156 while the body said 1,252, and I could not tell which of my two figures was right. The note was right and the issue body was wrong. Worth naming why the marker existed: I had previously produced and retracted a false finding on this very issue by reimplementing `scanLifecycleAnchors` instead of calling it. The critic called it. Same defect class, opposite outcome.

**`audit:terminal-share` — resolved. 97.491% of calls, and there is a trap.**

1,322 of 1,354 anchored rows are terminal. At the call denominator, **1,127 of 1,156 unique issue numbers are reachable only from terminal rows**; 29 are reachable from non-terminal rows, and **one issue is shared between a terminal and a non-terminal row**.

That shared anchor is the trap, and it is the kind of thing that ships as a silent coverage hole: an implementation that subtracts every issue number appearing in a terminal row would wrongly drop that issue. Rows must be filtered first, then issue numbers deduplicated. My write-back asked whether the share was large; it did not anticipate that the ordering of two set operations decides whether the optimisation is correct.

**`audit:drift-definition` — resolved. The target is true of this gate and false as stated.**

`buildLifecycleReport` partitions rows solely on `state === "OPEN"`, and Step 3 reports only non-terminal paths from `no_open_issue`. Its mismatch set is exactly *anchor has a non-open issue AND anchor path is non-terminal*. Filtering terminal rows before the state lookup preserves that set.

But the sentence I wrote — "terminal briefs cannot be lifecycle-drifted" — is false as a general lifecycle claim. A completed brief whose issue is still open **is** reverse drift; this gate simply does not test for it. So the narrowing is safe only against the invariant Step 3 happens to check today, and the equivalence breaks the moment Step 3 covers reverse drift, consults terminal issue state, exposes report totals, or filters issue numbers instead of rows.

That is a live #3156 concern rather than a settled one: the optimisation is coverage-preserving by coincidence of the current invariant, not by construction. Anything that narrows a gate on that basis has to say so out loud, or a later widening silently un-narrows it.

## The blocking finding kills my preferred direction

`An open-only paginated fetch removes the need to narrow` — `blocks-the-design`, accepted.

Measured against the live repository:

| Approach | Pages | Rows | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `state=all&per_page=100` (the body's direction 1) | 38 | 3,744 | 29.8 s |
| `state=open&per_page=100` | **6** | **558** | **4.2 s**, one subprocess |

Feeding that open-number set to the production scanner's 32 non-terminal anchor rows reproduced the same verdict: 29 candidates, zero mismatches. And the repository already contains a bounded pull-filtering REST issue-list implementation defaulting to open (`cache/fetch.ts:320-365`), though it currently spawns per page rather than once for the whole pagination.

So both of the body's leading directions are wrong in different ways. The literal all-state list still scales with total project history and misses the issue's own acceptance criterion. My preferred narrowing leaves 29 sequential subprocesses **and** takes on a coverage-narrowing proof burden that turns out to be unnecessary. One open-only paginated call keeps the full anchor set, avoids the #3156 argument entirely, and is measured at 4.2 seconds.

Treating absence from a complete open inventory as "non-open" is the inversion that makes it work, and it is also where the risk moves: the inventory must be parse-complete and fail closed, or a truncated page silently marks open issues as closed and inverts the gate. The footnote is right that this is now the load-bearing safety property — fail closed on command failure, malformed or non-array pages, pagination exhaustion, and buffer exhaustion, and ignore pull-request rows.

## Recut

- **Remedy**: one fail-closed, open-only paginated REST subprocess for the whole inventory. Retain the full anchor set. Treat any anchored issue absent from a complete open inventory as non-open. Terminal prefiltering only if that baseline is measured inadequate.
- **Correct the count**: 1,156 unique anchors, not 1,252, everywhere the current corpus is claimed.
